title: Lyrtech RD (Jan 2013 TCC) Tax Court of Canada Ruling
subject: Dispute over CCPC status and whether a related-party structure preserved eligibility for enhanced refundable SR&ED credits.
summary: Lyrtech RD Inc. v. The Queen, 2013 TCC 12, shows how a public corporation's spin-out of its R&D team into a trust-held subsidiary failed to secure Canadian-controlled private corporation status. The Tax Court of Canada held that Lyrtech Inc. exercised de facto control under subsection 256(5.1), denying the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED investment tax credits.
metaDescription: Review the January 2013 Tax Court of Canada decision for Lyrtech RD and its implications for Canadian SR&ED tax credit claims.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Overview of the Dispute and the Taxpayer's Claim

In Lyrtech RD Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2013 TCC 12 (Docket: 2009-1057(IT)G), handed down on January 24, 2013, the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) adjudicated a foundational dispute concerning the corporate eligibility requirements for Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program. Presided over by the Honourable Justice Réal Favreau following a three-day hearing in Quebec City, Quebec—and subsequently affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal on November 17, 2014 (2014 FCA 267, Docket: A-72-13), with leave to appeal dismissed by the Supreme Court of Canada on July 9, 2015 (SCC File No. 36259)—the decision examines the validity of a corporate "spin-out" reorganization designed to convert non-refundable 20% SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) into enhanced, 100% refundable 35% ITCs.

The appellant, Lyrtech RD Inc., originated from the corporate group of Technologies Lyre Inc., an engineering firm incorporated on June 26, 1991, by founders Louis Bélanger and Louis Chouinard to develop digital signal processors (DSPs), digital electronic circuits, and analog circuits. On March 9, 2000, Lyrtech Inc. was incorporated; on September 1, 2000, Technologies Lyre Inc. acquired control of Lyrtech Inc., and the two corporations merged that same day, with Lyrtech Inc. continuing the activities of Technologies Lyre Inc. Following a public offering prospectus filed on October 4, 2000, Lyrtech Inc. became a "public corporation" within the meaning of subsection 89(1) of the Income Tax Act (Canada), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA"), with a class of its shares listed on a designated Canadian stock exchange since October 4, 2000, and widely held: according to the management information circulars of Lyrtech Inc., no shareholder held more than 10% of its Class A shares, although the Federal Court of Appeal noted that Corriente Master Fund held slightly over 25,000,000 of the 243,725,724 issued and outstanding Class A voting shares, and no shareholder was able to elect a majority of the seven shareholder-elected directors of Lyrtech Inc.

Between 2000 and 2004, Lyrtech Inc. conducted extensive SR&ED activities and claimed basic ITCs at the statutory rate of 20%. However, because Lyrtech Inc. was a public corporation operating in a cumulative tax loss position, it had no Part I federal income tax payable against which to offset its non-refundable ITCs, rendering the tax credits illiquid and of no immediate financial benefit. To monetize its ongoing research expenditures, Lyrtech Inc. executed a multi-entity corporate and trust reorganization on May 30 and June 1, 2005, transferring its R&D workforce and tangible R&D equipment into a newly incorporated entity, Lyrtech RD Inc., whose voting shares were held entirely by an inter vivos discretionary trust, Fiducie Financière Lyrtech (FFL).

Following this restructuring, Lyrtech RD Inc. filed its corporate income tax returns for the 2005, 2006, and 2007 taxation years on the basis that it qualified as a "Canadian-controlled private corporation" (CCPC) under subsection 125(7) of the ITA. On that basis, the appellant claimed the additional 15% ITC rate supplement under subsection 127(10.1)—yielding a combined 35% SR&ED ITC rate—and claimed a cash refund of those credits as a "qualifying corporation" pursuant to subsections 127.1(1) and 127.1(2) of the ITA.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

By Notice of Assessment dated February 8, 2008, for the 2005 taxation year and Notices of Assessment dated July 9, 2008, for the 2006 and 2007 taxation years, the Minister of National Revenue, acting through the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), disallowed Lyrtech RD Inc.'s CCPC status, thereby denying both the 15% ITC addition under subsection 127(10.1) and the ITC refund under subsection 127.1(1).

The Crown mounted a two-tiered challenge to the reorganization. Under its primary argument concerning de facto control pursuant to subsection 256(5.1) of the ITA, the Minister contended that throughout the 2005, 2006, and 2007 taxation years, Lyrtech RD Inc. was controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by Lyrtech Inc., a public corporation. Specifically, the Crown argued that despite the interposition of the discretionary trust FFL as the registered holder of 100% of the appellant's voting shares, Lyrtech Inc. possessed and exercised direct and indirect operational, managerial, and economic influence that resulted in control in fact (de facto control) within the meaning of subsection 256(5.1) of the ITA, disqualifying the appellant from CCPC status under paragraph 125(7)(a).

In its first alternative argument, the Crown asserted deemed de jure control under subparagraph 251(5)(b)(i) of the ITA. The Respondent submitted that each of the corporate beneficiaries of FFL—namely 4296621 Canada Inc., 4296630 Canada Inc., and 4296648 Canada Inc., all of which were wholly owned directly or indirectly by Lyrtech Inc.—was "beneficially interested" in the trust under subsection 248(25) and consequently held a conditional right in equity or otherwise to acquire the voting shares of the appellant's capital stock. Under subparagraph 251(5)(b)(i), the Crown argued that this conditional right deemed Lyrtech Inc.'s subsidiaries to occupy the same position in relation to the control of the appellant as if they owned its voting shares directly, resulting in indirect de jure control by a public corporation. The Minister did not plead the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR) in section 245 of the ITA; the dispute was confined to the de facto control argument and the alternative deemed de jure control argument.
Governing Statutory Framework

The legal architecture governing the dispute centres on the intersection of the SR&ED investment tax credit provisions and the corporate control rules in the Income Tax Act (Canada) alongside federal corporate governance statutes.

headers: Statutory Role & Legal Mechanism in the Dispute

cells: Subsection 89(1) ITA
Defines a "public corporation" as a corporation resident in Canada whose class of shares is listed on a designated stock exchange in Canada.
Subsection 125(7) ITA ("CCPC")

Defines a "Canadian-controlled private corporation" as a private corporation that is a Canadian corporation other than a corporation "controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever", by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), or by any combination thereof.
Subsection 127(10.1) ITA

Grants an additional 15% Investment Tax Credit (over and above the base 20% SR&ED ITC under subsection 127(9)) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the expenditure limit, strictly restricted to a corporation that was throughout the year a CCPC.
Subsections 127.1(1) & 127.1(2) ITA

Provides for the cash refundability of ITCs ("refundable investment tax credit") to a "qualifying corporation," which is defined in paragraph 127.1(2)(a) as a corporation that is a CCPC throughout the particular taxation year and whose taxable income (together with associated corporations) for the preceding year does not exceed its business limit for that preceding year.
Subsection 256(5.1) ITA (De Facto Control)

Enacted in 1988, stipulates that where the expression "controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever" is used in the ITA, a corporation shall be considered to be so controlled by another corporation, person, or group of persons (the "controller") at any time where, at that time, the controller has any direct or indirect influence that, if exercised, would result in control in fact of the corporation.
Subparagraph 251(5)(b)(i) & Subsection 248(25) ITA

Deems a person who has a right under a contract, in equity or otherwise, either immediately or in the future and either absolutely or contingently, to, or to acquire, shares of the capital stock of a corporation (or to control the voting rights thereof) to be in the same position in relation to the control of the corporation as if the person owned the shares at that time. Subsection 248(25) defines when a person or partnership is "beneficially interested" in a trust.
Paragraph 256(1.2)(f) & Subsections 256(1.4), (6.1), (6.2) ITA

Sets out specific look-through attribution rules for shares held by a discretionary trust (deeming beneficiaries to own the shares for the purpose of the associated corporation rules in subsections 256(1) to (5)), as well as rules governing simultaneous and multi-tier corporate control.
Subsection 146(2) CBCA

Permits a sole shareholder of a corporation governed by the Canada Business Corporations Act to execute a written declaration that restricts, in whole or in part, the powers of the directors to manage, or supervise the management of, the business and affairs of the corporation.

body.text: The Court's Final Holding
Justice Favreau dismissed Lyrtech RD Inc.'s appeals for the 2005, 2006, and 2007 taxation years with costs to the Respondent, upholding the Minister's reassessments in full.

On the Crown's alternative argument under subparagraph 251(5)(b)(i), the Court actually ruled in favour of the taxpayer's technical interpretation. Justice Favreau held at paragraphs 54 to 59 that although the corporate beneficiaries of FFL were "beneficially interested" in the discretionary trust under subsection 248(25), the beneficial interest of each capital beneficiary of FFL was too aleatory, uncertain or indirect to constitute a right to the shares of the appellant within the contemplation of paragraph 251(5)(b), and conferred no right on its holder to acquire shares of the appellant. Furthermore, the look-through rule in paragraph 256(1.2)(f) applies only for the purposes of subsections 256(1) to (5) governing associated corporations and does not apply directly to the definition of a CCPC in subsection 125(7).

However, on the primary issue, the Court delivered a decisive holding against the taxpayer. First, the TCC rejected the appellant's legal submission that a finding of de jure control in the hands of the FFL trustees precluded an inquiry into de facto control by Lyrtech Inc. Justice Favreau held that de jure control and de facto control coexist simultaneously across all provisions of the ITA utilizing the phrase "controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever". Second, evaluating the totality of the governance, contractual, operational, and economic evidence against the factors in CRA Interpretation Bulletin IT-64R4 and the case law—including Mimetix Pharmaceuticals Inc. v. Canada (affirmed 2003 FCA 106), L.D.G. 2000 Inc. v. Canada, and Duha Printers (Western) Ltd. v. Canada—the Court concluded that Lyrtech Inc. exercised a dominant economic influence over Lyrtech RD Inc. Because Lyrtech Inc. held de facto control over the appellant under subsection 256(5.1), Lyrtech RD Inc. was not a CCPC under subsection 125(7) and was statutorily barred from claiming the 15% ITC supplement and cash refunds. No GAAR argument was pleaded; on further appeal, the Federal Court of Appeal (2014 FCA 267), having upheld the de facto control finding, held that there was no need to address the Crown's alternative subparagraph 251(5)(b)(i) argument.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of Lyrtech RD Inc.'s enhanced SR&ED tax credit claims did not stem from a failure to perform scientific or technological development in the laboratory; rather, it arose from a pervasive failure to align the legal, governance, contractual, and financial reality of the R&D entity with the statutory requirements of the Income Tax Act. Tax planners had constructed a formalistic de jure shell while leaving Lyrtech RD Inc. operationally, contractually, and financially captive to Lyrtech Inc. A granular examination of the record reveals seven interlocking legal, contractual, and documentation deficiencies that proved fatal at trial.
The Governance Trap: Trust Deed Removal Mechanics and the CBCA Subsection 146(2) Declaration

To sever de jure control between Lyrtech Inc. (the public parent) and Lyrtech RD Inc. (the R&D subsidiary), tax counsel interposed a multi-tiered chain of corporations and a discretionary trust on May 30 and June 1, 2005. Lyrtech Inc. incorporated a wholly-owned subsidiary, 4296621 Canada Inc., subscribing for 400 Class A shares for $400; 4296621 in turn incorporated two wholly-owned subsidiaries, 4296630 Canada Inc. and 4296648 Canada Inc., subscribing for 100 Class A shares for $100 in each. On June 1, 2005, 4296621 settled Fiducie Financière Lyrtech (FFL) with a $200 contribution, designating 4296630, 4296648, and Lyrtech RD Inc. as income beneficiaries, and 4296630, 4296648, and 4296621 as capital beneficiaries. FFL then subscribed for 100 Class A shares and 100 Class B shares of Lyrtech RD Inc. for $100 in each case (the Class A shares being the only voting shares of the appellant), holding 100% of the appellant's voting stock.

Relying on the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in M.N.R. v. Consolidated Holding Co., the appellant argued that where voting shares of a corporation are held by a trust, de jure control resides exclusively with the trustees who possess the legal authority to bind the trust. Furthermore, to insulate the appellant from any argument that Lyrtech Inc. could influence the appellant's board of directors, the trustees of FFL executed a sole shareholder declaration on June 1, 2005, under subsection 146(2) of the Canada Business Corporations Act (CBCA), withdrawing all managerial and supervisory powers from Lyrtech RD Inc.'s board of directors and assuming those powers themselves.

This governance mechanism backfired catastrophically due to two structural flaws embedded in the constitutive documents and personnel appointments. First, there was a complete identity of directors, officers, and trustees across the corporate group. The initial trustees of FFL were Miguel Caron, Louis Bélanger, and Vincent Bélanger, with Vincent Bélanger ceasing to be a trustee as of June 17, 2005, leaving only Miguel Caron and Louis Bélanger. As of June 8, 2005, Miguel Caron and Louis Bélanger were concurrently the sole directors of Lyrtech RD Inc., 4296621, 4296630, and 4296648, as well as the two non-independent directors among the seven members of the board of directors of Lyrtech Inc., where Miguel Caron was also president and chief executive officer and Louis N. Bélanger held positions including vice-chairman of the board and head of technology. Moreover, every executive officer of Lyrtech RD Inc. was identical to that of Lyrtech Inc.: Miguel Caron served as President of both entities, Alain Landry served as Vice-President of Finance and Human Resources of both, Daniel Bellemare served as Comptroller of both, and Sylvie Coulombe served as Secretary of both.

Second, and most damningly, the trust deed establishing FFL contained an explicit automatic disqualification clause stipulating that a trustee ceased to be a trustee of FFL the moment that individual ceased to be a director of Lyrtech Inc., and that the number of FFL trustees could not exceed the number of directors of Lyrtech Inc. Citing Duha Printers (Western) Ltd. v. Canada, Justice Favreau emphasized that external constitutive documents—specifically trust deeds and shareholder declarations—are vital in determining corporate control. Because the FFL trustees had assumed all directorial powers over Lyrtech RD Inc. via the subsection 146(2) CBCA declaration, and because the trust deed tied trustee status to directorship of Lyrtech Inc. (only directors of Lyrtech Inc. were eligible to become trustees, and a trustee ceased to hold office upon ceasing to be a director of Lyrtech Inc.), Justice Favreau concluded that the appellant was indirectly controlled by the two non-independent directors among the seven members of the board of directors of Lyrtech Inc., so that the controlling mind of the appellant was structurally tied to the board of Lyrtech Inc.
Misconception of Statutory Control: Simultaneous Coexistence of De Jure and De Facto Control

A foundational legal error committed by the appellant's advisors was the assumption that establishing valid de jure control in the hands of Canadian-resident individual trustees automatically immunized the corporation against a finding of de facto control by a public corporation. The appellant argued before the TCC that de jure control and de facto control cannot be analyzed or exist simultaneously unless an express statutory deeming rule mandates such an inquiry.

Justice Favreau dismantled this proposition by tracing the legislative history and purpose of subsection 256(5.1), which was enacted in 1988 specifically to broaden the test of corporate control beyond the strict de jure standard where a dominant entity possesses influence that, when exercised, results in actual control. Referring to CRA Interpretation Bulletin IT-64R4 and subsections 256(6.1) and (6.2), the Court confirmed that whenever the ITA employs the phrase "controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever"—as it does explicitly in paragraph 125(7)(a) in defining a CCPC—Parliament intends to capture both de jure control and de facto control simultaneously. Consequently, even though the trustees of FFL held de jure control over Lyrtech RD Inc., Lyrtech Inc. simultaneously held de facto control under subsection 256(5.1), which was fully sufficient to trigger the CCPC exclusion in subsection 125(7).
Contractual Subjugation, Absence of Intellectual Property, and the 60-Day Termination Clause

The contractual architecture governing the SR&ED projects between Lyrtech Inc. and Lyrtech RD Inc. demonstrated complete commercial and technical subordination. Under the June 1, 2005 asset transfer, Lyrtech Inc. transferred its tangible R&D assets and 43 R&D employees to Lyrtech RD Inc., but explicitly excluded its intellectual property. Lyrtech Inc. retained legal and beneficial ownership of all background patents, proprietary DSP architectures, and core technologies.

Concurrently on June 1, 2005, Lyrtech Inc. and Lyrtech RD Inc. executed an indeterminate-term research contract under which Lyrtech RD Inc. was engaged solely to pursue ongoing R&D on Lyrtech Inc.'s owned and patented technologies. In consideration for its R&D activities, Lyrtech RD Inc. was not granted autonomous rights to exploit the foreground IP in the open market; instead, its compensation was restricted to a contingent royalty of 10% of Lyrtech Inc.'s product sales revenue and 25% of Lyrtech Inc.'s licensing revenue.

Critically, the research contract contained a unilateral termination clause permitting Lyrtech Inc. to terminate the agreement upon giving 60 days' notice. Because Lyrtech RD Inc. owned no underlying IP, had no external sales force or commercial infrastructure, and had no client other than Lyrtech Inc., exercising the 60-day termination clause would instantly extinguish the appellant's sole source of revenue and render its 43-person engineering workforce idle. Evaluating the six general factors of de facto control set out in paragraph 23 of Interpretation Bulletin IT-64R4—which include commercial or contractual relationships leading to economic dependence on a single supplier or customer and possession of a unique expertise required to operate the business, supplemented by the composition of the board of directors and the control of day-to-day management—Justice Favreau identified this unilateral 60-day termination right over a single-client R&D subsidiary as a classic manifestation of dominant economic influence under subsection 256(5.1).
Financial Captivity and the Circular $1,016,437 Demand Promissory Note

The capitalization of Lyrtech RD Inc. further cemented its economic dependence on the Lyrtech corporate group. Whereas FFL subscribed for 100 Class A shares (the only voting shares) and 100 Class B shares for a nominal $200, the actual operating R&D assets transferred by Lyrtech Inc. on June 1, 2005, were valued at $1,016,437. In exchange for those assets, Lyrtech RD Inc. issued 1,016,437 Class C shares of its capital stock to Lyrtech Inc. and immediately redeemed them by issuing a demand promissory note for $1,016,437 payable to Lyrtech Inc.

Through a pre-ordained sequence of transactions on the same day, Lyrtech Inc. used the $1,016,437 demand note to purchase shares in 4296621; 4296621 transferred the note to 4296630; and 4296630 paid a $1,016,437 dividend on its Class E shares held by FFL by delivering the demand promissory note to FFL. As a result, Lyrtech RD Inc. began its corporate existence burdened by a $1,016,437 debt payable on demand to FFL—whose trustees were the senior directors of Lyrtech Inc. and whose capital beneficiaries were Lyrtech Inc.'s wholly-owned subsidiaries (4296621, 4296630, and 4296648). Factor (b) of paragraph 23 of IT-64R4 lists ownership of a large debt that may become payable on demand; although Justice Favreau did not single out the demand note in his reasons, he found that the appellant was undercapitalized, could not operate without advances of funds from Lyrtech Inc. (around $2,037,481 from June 1 to December 31, 2005), and relied on bank credit facilities for which Lyrtech Inc. stood surety, all of which supported the finding of de facto control. Furthermore, the financial statements of the corporations were consolidated into Lyrtech Inc.'s public financial reporting, reflecting accounting recognition of Lyrtech Inc.'s economic dominance.
Operational Commingling and Deficient Contemporaneous Cost Documentation

The evidentiary record before the TCC also revealed a stark absence of operational separateness and contemporaneous intercompany cost documentation between Lyrtech Inc. and Lyrtech RD Inc. Following the June 1, 2005 restructuring, Lyrtech RD Inc.'s 43 engineers continued occupying space in the exact same premises rented by Lyrtech Inc. for $15,848 per month. As of January 24, 2007—more than a year and a half after the spin-out—there was still no written lease or sublease agreement between Lyrtech Inc. and the appellant, and the appellant recorded zero rental expenses for the period from June 1 to December 31, 2005.

Rather than maintaining separate vendor contracts, independent accounting ledgers, and activity-based SR&ED cost tracking, the appellant absorbed portions of Lyrtech Inc.'s general business expenses allocated mechanically on the basis of an employee headcount ratio of 43/79. Because this 43/79 ratio was applied indiscriminately without arm's-length commercial scrutiny, Lyrtech RD Inc. assumed part of the life insurance premium for some directors although Lyrtech Inc. was the sole beneficiary of the policy, part of the premium for insurance covering damage to equipment of which Lyrtech Inc. was the sole beneficiary, part of the fees paid to directors attending meetings of the Lyrtech Inc. board and of the remuneration of its chairman, Pierre Lortie, and part of the accounting fees related to the audit of Lyrtech Inc.'s consolidated financial statements. No genuinely independent corporation governed by autonomous fiduciaries would agree to subsidize life insurance policies payable exclusively to its client or pay for its client's consolidated public-company audit fees.
Intersection with Substantive SR&ED Eligibility and Funded Research Rules

From a technical SR&ED tax advisory perspective, the structural and contractual deficiencies exposed in Lyrtech RD Inc. also highlight critical vulnerabilities across the broader statutory SR&ED regime in sections 37 and 127 and subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Under subsection 127(18) of the ITA, read with the definitions of "qualified expenditure" and "contract payment" in subsection 127(9), a taxpayer performing SR&ED in Canada must reduce its qualified SR&ED expenditures by the amount of any "contract payment" received or receivable for performing SR&ED on behalf of another person resident in Canada. In Lyrtech RD Inc., the compensation of the appellant was structured not as fee-for-service R&D reimbursements but as a contingent share of future income (10% of the income from sales of products resulting from the R&D work and 25% of the income from licences), so that it was paid on the basis of sales rather than the expenses it incurred, while it earned no royalty income and was financed by advances of funds from Lyrtech Inc.; the courts did not address the contract payment rules. However, structuring compensation as a contingent royalty tied exclusively to the parent's owned technologies—coupled with a 60-day termination clause and zero IP ownership—created the exact economic dependence that triggered subsection 256(5.1).

Similarly, while the appeals in Lyrtech RD Inc. concerned only CCPC status under subsections 125(7) and 256(5.1)—the appellant did not contest the adjustments made by the Minister to its claimed SR&ED expenditures, and the eligibility of the underlying DSP engineering under subsection 248(1) was not in issue, the Court's findings on operational commingling carry direct implications for substantive SR&ED audits. Under Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence, a claimant must prove through contemporaneous documentation the existence of technological uncertainty, specific technological hypotheses formulated to overcome that uncertainty, a systematic process of experimentation and analysis, resulting technological advancement, and contemporaneous records generated as the work progressed. Furthermore, under section 37, expenditures must be directly attributable to, or constitute a specifically identifiable incremental cost of, the claimant's SR&ED prosecution. When an R&D subsidiary uses an arbitrary headcount ratio (such as Lyrtech's 43/79 split) to allocate parent-company overhead and fails to maintain independent project governance logs showing who directed the technical hypotheses, CRA auditors can challenge not only CCPC status under subsection 256(5.1), but also the deductibility of the allocated expenditures under section 37 and the eligibility of the underlying technical claim under subsection 248(1).
Second- and Third-Order Jurisprudential Impact in Canada

The TCC's analysis in Lyrtech RD Inc. (2013 TCC 12), affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal (2014 FCA 267), triggered a major doctrinal evolution in Canadian corporate tax law. In Silicon Graphics Ltd. v. Canada (2002 FCA 260), the FCA had previously articulated a narrow threshold for de facto control at paragraph 67, stating that a controller must have "the clear right and ability to effect a significant change in the board of directors or the powers of the board of directors or to influence in a very direct way the shareholders who would otherwise have the ability to elect the board of directors". In Lyrtech, Justice Favreau relied on operational and economic dependence factors (derived from Mimetix Pharmaceuticals Inc. v. Canada and IT-64R4) alongside the trust-deed governance link to establish de facto control, and the FCA—while reiterating that the basic principle is set out in Silicon Graphics at paragraph 67, as clarified in 9044 2807 Québec Inc. v. Canada (2004 FCA 23)—found no palpable and overriding error in that conclusion.

When the Federal Court of Appeal subsequently held in McGillivray Restaurant Ltd. v. The Queen (2016 FCA 99) that the factors relevant to de facto control must include a legally enforceable right and ability to effect a change to the board of directors or its powers, or to influence the shareholders who have that right and ability, and that Mimetix and Plomberie J.C. Langlois Inc. ought not to be followed to the extent they prescribed an inconsistent test—thereby narrowing the economic-dependence approach on which Lyrtech had relied, Parliament intervened directly by enacting subsection 256(5.11) of the ITA, announced in the federal budget of March 22, 2017 and enacted by the Budget Implementation Act, 2017, No. 2 (S.C. 2017, c. 33, s. 79, assented to December 14, 2017). Subsection 256(5.11), applicable to taxation years beginning after March 21, 2017, legislatively reversed McGillivray and restored a broad multi-factor approach of the kind applied in Lyrtech, mandating that a court determining de facto control under subsection 256(5.1) must take into consideration all factors that are relevant in the circumstances and is not limited to whether the taxpayer has a legally enforceable right or ability to effect a change in the board of directors or its powers. Consequently, a holistic multi-factor analysis of the kind Justice Favreau undertook in Lyrtech RD Inc. (2013 TCC 12) is consistent with the statutory standard now set out in subsection 256(5.11).
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and legal requirement examined in Lyrtech RD Inc. v. The Queen (2013 TCC 12) against the specific structural or evidentiary failures of the appellant and the governing standard of proof established by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Taxpayer's Structural, Contractual, or Evidentiary Failure
The Tax Court of Canada's Standard of Proof & Legal Holding

cells: Qualification as a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC)
Subsection 125(7) & Subsection 89(1) ITA

The appellant claimed CCPC status solely on the basis that it was a private Canadian corporation whose shares (all 100 Class A shares, its only voting shares, and 100 Class B shares) were legally registered in the name of a Canadian-resident discretionary trust (FFL), ignoring the influence exercised by its public parent, Lyrtech Inc.

To qualify as a CCPC throughout the taxation year, the taxpayer bears the burden of proving on a balance of probabilities that it is neither controlled in law (de jure) nor controlled in fact (de facto)—"directly or indirectly in any manner whatever"—by one or more public corporations or non-residents.
Entitlement to Enhanced 35% SR&ED ITC Rate and 100% Cash Refundability
Subsection 127(10.1) & Subsections 127.1(1), 127.1(2) ITA

The appellant claimed the additional 15% ITC supplement and full cash refundability for its 2005, 2006, and 2007 taxation years despite being economically and managerially integrated into a public corporation (Lyrtech Inc.) that was only entitled to a non-refundable 20% ITC rate.

Strict statutory compliance is required: CCPC status must be maintained throughout the entire taxation year. Disqualification from CCPC status under s. 125(7) automatically extinguishes entitlement to the 15% addition under s. 127(10.1) and "qualifying corporation" refund status under s. 127.1(2).
Simultaneous Coexistence of De Jure and De Facto Control
Subsection 256(5.1), Subsections 256(6.1)–(6.2) & Subsection 125(7) ITA

The appellant argued that because FFL held de jure control, the Court was legally barred from conducting a simultaneous analysis of de facto control in the absence of an explicit statutory cross-reference.

The Court held that de jure control and de facto control are not mutually exclusive; they coexist simultaneously for all provisions of the ITA using the phrase "controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever". Establishing de jure control in a trust does not shield the taxpayer from a finding of de facto control by a public company.
Independence of Corporate Governance & Constitutive Trust Instruments
Subsection 256(5.1) ITA; Subsection 146(2) CBCA; Consolidated Holding Co.; Duha Printers

FFL's trustees executed a s. 146(2) CBCA sole shareholder declaration withdrawing all powers from the appellant's board and vesting them in the trustees. However, the FFL trust deed stipulated that a trustee automatically ceased to be a trustee upon ceasing to be a director of Lyrtech Inc., and all officers (President, VP Finance/HR, Comptroller, Secretary) were identical across both entities.

Under Duha Printers and s. 256(5.1), the Court examines trust deeds, unanimous shareholder declarations, and board/management composition. Where the trust deed ties trustee status to directorship of the public corporation, so that the subsidiary is indirectly controlled by the non-independent directors of the public corporation, and where management is identical, the public corporation holds direct structural influence over the subsidiary's controlling mind.
Absence of Contingent Share Acquisition Rights in a Discretionary Trust
Subparagraph 251(5)(b)(i) & Subsection 248(25) ITA

The Crown argued that Lyrtech Inc.'s wholly-owned subsidiaries (4296621, 4296630, 4296648), as discretionary beneficiaries of FFL under s. 248(25), held a conditional right in equity under s. 251(5)(b)(i) to acquire the appellant's voting shares. (Note: The taxpayer succeeded on this narrow issue).

At paras. 54–59, the Court held that being "beneficially interested" in a discretionary trust under s. 248(25) does not confer a "right" under s. 251(5)(b)(i) to acquire the underlying shares held by the trust, because the interest of the capital beneficiaries was too aleatory, uncertain or indirect to be a right to the shares of the appellant; the FCA found it unnecessary to address this alternative argument on appeal.
Commercial Autonomy & Freedom from Economic Dependence
Subsection 256(5.1) ITA; Mimetix Pharmaceuticals; Silicon Graphics; CRA IT-64R4 (para. 23)

The appellant had only one client (Lyrtech Inc.); owned zero background IP; operated under a Research Contract that Lyrtech Inc. could unilaterally terminate on 60 days' notice; relied on royalties (10% of sales, 25% of licensing) from Lyrtech Inc.'s products; and owed a $1,016,437 demand promissory note held by FFL.

Under s. 256(5.1) (and subsequently codified in s. 256(5.11)), the Court evaluates economic and contractual reality. Where a single client controls all underlying IP, holds a 60-day termination right capable of destroying the taxpayer's business, and is tied to substantial demand debt, the client exercises dominant economic influence amounting to de facto control.
Operational Separateness & Contemporaneous Expense Documentation
Subsection 256(5.1), Section 37 & Subsection 127(9) ITA

The appellant operated inside Lyrtech Inc.'s leased premises ($15,848/month) without a written lease and recorded zero rent in 2005; its financial statements were consolidated with Lyrtech Inc.; and it absorbed 43/79ths of Lyrtech Inc.'s expenses, including life insurance naming Lyrtech Inc. as sole beneficiary and Lyrtech Inc.'s public audit fees.

A taxpayer asserting independent corporate status and claiming SR&ED expenditures must prove genuine operational separation and arm's-length commercial dealings through contemporaneous documentation. Paying a parent company's audit fees and life insurance premiums via an arbitrary headcount ratio evidences complete managerial subordination.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial holdings of Lyrtech RD Inc. v. The Queen (2013 TCC 12) and the statutory requirements of subsections 125(7), 256(5.1), 256(5.11), 37(1), 127(9), 127(10.1), 127.1(1), and 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (Canada) into actionable tax and technical governance protocols, the following two applied industry case studies demonstrate how Canadian taxpayers facing these exact pitfalls must restructure their corporate governance, intercompany contracts, financial accounting, and technical SR&ED documentation.
Case Study 1: Advanced Digital Signal Processing (DSP) & RF Hardware Spin-Out (The "St-Laurent Photon-DSP" Restructuring)
Baseline Fact Pattern & Identified Legal Pitfalls

St-Laurent Telecom Corp. ("SLT PubCo") is a TSX-listed Canadian public corporation based in Montreal, Quebec, specializing in optical and radio-frequency (RF) telecommunications hardware. Operating in a multi-year tax loss position, SLT PubCo cannot monetize its non-refundable federal SR&ED ITCs. Although subsection 127(10.1), as amended by the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3, assented to March 26, 2026), now extends the enhanced credit to an "eligible Canadian public corporation" as defined in subsection 127(9), the $6 million expenditure limit of such a corporation under subsection 127(10.6) is reduced where its average annual revenue for the three preceding taxation years exceeds $15 million and is nil once that average reaches $75 million; SLT PubCo's average annual revenue exceeds $75 million, so its expenditure limit is nil. Its engineers are initiating a high-risk R&D project ("Project Ultra-MIMO") to develop a real-time adaptive pre-distortion algorithm and custom FPGA/DSP board architecture capable of eliminating non-linear signal distortion across ultra-wideband 6G transceivers operating at sub-terahertz frequencies.

Seeking to access the 35% refundable federal SR&ED ITC, SLT PubCo's advisors propose spinning out the 38-engineer DSP team into a new corporation, St-Laurent RD Lab Inc. ("RD Lab"), whose voting shares will be owned by a discretionary trust (Fiducie Innovation St-Laurent) settled by a subsidiary of SLT PubCo. Under the initial draft plan, the trustees of the trust are the CEO and CFO of SLT PubCo, who execute a subsection 146(2) CBCA unanimous shareholder declaration assuming all powers of RD Lab's board, while the trust deed requires trustees to be sitting officers or directors of SLT PubCo. SLT PubCo transfers its lab oscilloscopes and test benches to RD Lab for redeemable preferred shares, redeemed immediately via a $1.5 million demand promissory note cycled into the trust, while SLT PubCo retains all background and foreground IP. Furthermore, SLT PubCo grants RD Lab a research service contract terminable by SLT PubCo on 60 days' notice, compensating RD Lab via an 8% royalty on future transceiver sales. Finally, RD Lab remains in SLT PubCo's Montreal facility without a sublease, shares the same executive officers, allocates overhead on a 38/85 headcount ratio, and relies on high-level quarterly milestone summaries rather than granular, hypothesis-driven experimentation logs.

Under Lyrtech RD Inc. (2013 TCC 12) and subsections 256(5.1) and 256(5.11) of the ITA, this proposed structure is guaranteed to fail a CRA audit. SLT PubCo holds de facto control over RD Lab through the trust deed's director-tie-in clause, identical management, the $1.5 million demand note, the 60-day termination right, IP captivity, and operational commingling, disqualifying RD Lab from CCPC status under subsection 125(7). Moreover, even if CCPC status were preserved, any R&D service payments from SLT PubCo to RD Lab risk characterization as a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9), grinding down RD Lab's qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar, while the arbitrary 38/85 overhead allocation and weak technical logs risk disallowance under section 37 and subsection 248(1).
Step 1: Corporate Ownership & Governance Restructuring (Eliminating De Facto Control under Subsections 125(7), 256(5.1), and 256(5.11))

To qualify RD Lab as a genuine CCPC throughout the taxation year under subsection 125(7), the artificial discretionary trust structure (Fiducie Innovation St-Laurent) settled by a public-company subsidiary must be abandoned entirely. Instead, RD Lab must be capitalized as an independent Canadian private corporation controlled both de jure and de facto by Canadian-resident private investors, independent engineering founders, or an arm's-length Canadian private equity or venture capital group. At least 75% of the voting shares of RD Lab should be subscribed for at fair market value by Canadian-resident founding engineers—who permanently resign from any executive or directorial role at SLT PubCo—alongside independent Canadian angel or private venture investors. SLT PubCo's equity participation, if any, must be strictly capped at a passive, non-controlling minority interest (such as 20% or less of voting common shares) with no special veto rights, casting votes, or options to acquire additional shares under subparagraph 251(5)(b)(i).

Concurrently, RD Lab must establish an independent three- or five-member Board of Directors elected by the Canadian private shareholders. No director or officer of SLT PubCo may sit on RD Lab's Board or serve as an officer (President, VP Finance, Comptroller, or Secretary) of RD Lab. If a Unanimous Shareholder Agreement (USA) is utilized among the private shareholders, it must not confer any directorial veto, appointment right, or removal lever upon SLT PubCo, and no declaration under subsection 146(2) of the CBCA may vest managerial powers in fiduciaries tied to SLT PubCo. Furthermore, RD Lab must not acquire equipment from SLT PubCo in exchange for a demand promissory note. Instead, RD Lab should finance its laboratory equipment through arm's-length commercial equipment leasing, Canadian bank financing, or long-term fixed-maturity subordinated debentures (such as a 5-year fixed term with no demand feature and market-rate interest). Consequently, SLT PubCo will not control RD Lab under International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS 10) and will not consolidate RD Lab's financial statements.
Step 2: Commercial & Contractual Architecture (Severing Economic Dependence and Navigating Subsection 127(9) "Contract Payment" Rules)

To eliminate the economic dependence that proved fatal in Lyrtech RD Inc. and avoid the "contract payment" exclusion under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, RD Lab's commercial model must be transformed from a captive contract-research department into an autonomous Intellectual Property (IP) development and licensing enterprise. Rather than performing R&D on SLT PubCo's retained patents, RD Lab must either develop its own clean-sheet proprietary DSP/FPGA IP from inception or acquire outright ownership (or an irrevocable, perpetual, worldwide exclusive license) of the baseline background IP at fair market value. All foreground patents, VHDL/Verilog source code, and mask works generated during Project Ultra-MIMO must vest 100% in RD Lab.

Furthermore, RD Lab's corporate mandate and commercial agreements must explicitly permit and require it to license its adaptive pre-distortion DSP cores to multiple domestic and international customers across broader verticals, including satellite communications, medical imaging hardware, radar systems, and telecommunications OEMs. In its commercial licensing agreement with SLT PubCo, the 60-day unilateral termination clause must be completely eliminated. Instead, the agreement should be structured as a multi-year commercial IP licensing and product supply agreement terminable only for uncured material breach following a 180-day cure period. To preserve RD Lab's 35% refundable ITC base against the "contract payment" grind under subsection 127(9), RD Lab must fund its own SR&ED using its private equity capital and bank facilities, bear 100% of the technological and financial risk of failure, and enter into a standard commercial product supply or post-development commercial technology license with SLT PubCo. Because SLT PubCo is contracting to purchase commercialized standard DSP modules or non-exclusive commercial software licenses after development—rather than contracting for the performance of SR&ED on its behalf—the commercial revenues do not constitute "contract payments" under subsection 127(9).
Step 3: Operational Separateness & Financial Cost-Allocation Documentation (Section 37 & Form T661 Compliance)

To cure the evidentiary failures identified by Justice Favreau regarding shared premises and the arbitrary 43/79 expense allocation, RD Lab must implement rigorous operational and accounting separation. Ideally, RD Lab should lease physically separate laboratory premises from an unrelated third-party landlord. If RD Lab subleases space within the same building as SLT PubCo for access to specialized anechoic RF chambers, the parties must execute a formal, contemporaneous written commercial sublease prior to occupancy, specifying demarcated physical square footage, keycard-restricted access, and a fixed market rental rate per square foot paid monthly.

In addition, RD Lab must maintain its own independent general ledger, payroll registry, vendor contracts, property and casualty insurance policies, and independent external accounting firm. Under no circumstances may RD Lab pay any portion of SLT PubCo's executive life insurance, equipment insurance, or public-company audit fees. For SR&ED expenditure tracking on Form T661, RD Lab should elect to use the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA rather than the Traditional Method, thereby eliminating disputes over allocated facility overhead. Each of the 38 engineers must complete contemporaneous weekly digital timesheets tied to specific SR&ED project codes, strictly distinguishing eligible experimental development under paragraph (c) of the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) from non-eligible commercial routine engineering, debugging, or production support.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation & Experimentation Tracking (Satisfying Subsection 248(1))

To substantiate both that RD Lab's internal technical leadership independently directs the R&D—reinforcing the absence of de facto control by SLT PubCo—and that Project Ultra-MIMO satisfies the statutory criteria for SR&ED under subsection 248(1), RD Lab must institute a mandatory Technical Governance and Experimentation Protocol. Prior to commencing code architecture, RD Lab's Principal Investigator must document in a dated Technological Baseline Dossier why standard off-the-shelf Volterra-series digital pre-distortion (DPD) algorithms and existing commercial FPGA lookup tables fail when applied to 20 GHz instantaneous bandwidth at 140 GHz carrier frequencies, specifically documenting the system-level conflict between memory-effect compensation accuracy, FPGA logic-gate propagation latency (a 50 ns end-to-end budget), and thermal power dissipation (a 25 W board-level envelope).

Every subsequent engineering sprint in RD Lab's version-control and issue-tracking system (Git and Jira) must be anchored to a testable technological hypothesis formulated to overcome that uncertainty. For example, Hypothesis H-04 should state that implementing a pruned polyphase neural-polynomial hybrid architecture with dynamic 6-bit fixed-point quantization will reduce FPGA DSP-slice utilization by 42% while maintaining an Adjacent Channel Power Ratio (ACPR) below −45 dBc across thermal drift from −40°C to +85°C. Engineers must then log every simulation run (MATLAB/Simulink), hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) RF test bench vector capture, failed synthesis build, and bit-error-rate (BER) measurement directly into immutable, date-stamped laboratory notebooks signed off exclusively by RD Lab's internal Chief Technology Officer. Each entry must record the test parameters, the quantitative divergence between predicted and observed ACPR and latency metrics, the analytical conclusion explaining why a given quantization scheme failed, and the causal modification leading to the next hypothesis.
Case Study 2: Biopharmaceutical Drug Delivery Platform & Trust-Held Joint Venture (The "Boréal Nanomedicine" Structure)
Baseline Fact Pattern & Identified Legal Pitfalls

Boréal BioPharma Inc. ("Boréal Parent") is a Canadian private biotechnology corporation that is controlled 60% by a United States pharmaceutical conglomerate, a non-resident person. Because Boréal Parent is controlled by a non-resident, it is excluded from CCPC status under paragraph 125(7)(a) of the ITA and can only claim non-refundable basic federal SR&ED ITCs.

To develop a novel lipid-polymer hybrid nanoparticle (LPHN) platform capable of crossing the blood-brain barrier (BBB) for targeted mRNA delivery ("Project Neuro-Carrier"), tax advisors incorporate a separate Canadian entity, Boréal RD Solutions Inc. ("Boréal RD"). To avoid non-resident control under subsection 125(7), 100% of Boréal RD's voting shares are issued to a Canadian family trust (Fiducie Scientifique Boréal) whose trustees are two Canadian-resident executives of Boréal Parent, while Boréal Parent's wholly-owned Canadian subsidiary is named as a discretionary capital and income beneficiary of the trust. Under this initial structure, the trust deed empowers Boréal Parent (as "Protector" of the trust) to replace any trustee at any time, and contains an automatic removal clause if a trustee leaves Boréal Parent's employ. Additionally, Boréal Parent holds an option under a side letter to acquire 100% of the shares of Boréal RD from the trust at nominal book value upon completion of Phase I preclinical trials. Boréal RD has no wet-lab lease of its own, operates inside Boréal Parent's GLP facility without intercompany billing for eight months, shares the same VP Finance and Comptroller, and receives 100% of its operating cash via weekly advances from Boréal Parent under a Master Research Agreement that Boréal Parent can cancel on 30 days' notice. In the laboratory, technicians screen hundreds of lipid formulations using standard high-throughput assays without recording distinct scientific hypotheses or distinguishing routine formulation screening from systematic investigation of molecular structure-activity relationships.

This arrangement suffers from three fatal legal defects under Canadian tax law. First, it triggers deemed de jure control under subparagraph 251(5)(b)(i) of the ITA. Unlike in Lyrtech RD Inc. where the Crown relied solely on the beneficiaries' discretionary status under subsection 248(25)—which Justice Favreau held at paragraphs 54 to 59 did not constitute a right to acquire shares under subparagraph 251(5)(b)(i)—here Boréal Parent holds an explicit contractual option under a side letter to acquire Boréal RD's shares from the trust. Under subparagraph 251(5)(b)(i), Boréal Parent (a corporation controlled by a non-resident) is deemed to occupy the same position in relation to control of Boréal RD as if it owned the shares directly, destroying CCPC status via indirect de jure control. Second, even without the share option, Boréal Parent's power as "Protector" and employer to remove the trustees, combined with identical financial officers, sole-client dependency, 30-day contract termination rights, and unleased shared wet-lab facilities, establishes de facto control under subsections 256(5.1) and 256(5.11) following the exact ratio decidendi of Lyrtech RD Inc. (2013 TCC 12). Third, the weekly cash advances under the Master Research Agreement constitute "contract payments" under subsection 127(9) that eliminate Boréal RD's qualified SR&ED expenditure pool, while undocumented high-throughput screening without hypothesis-driven analysis fails the definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1) as routine trial-and-error testing.
Step 1: Trust & Corporate Governance Remediation (Satisfying Subparagraph 251(5)(b)(i), Subsection 125(7), and Subsection 256(5.1))

If a Canadian family or founder trust is utilized to hold voting shares of Boréal RD, its legal architecture must be completely purged of any direct or indirect control levers held by Boréal Parent or its non-resident parent. Neither Boréal Parent nor any corporation related to or controlled by Boréal Parent may be named as a capital or income beneficiary of the trust. Furthermore, the side-letter option must be cancelled ab initio or prior to the taxation year, and no option, right of first refusal, convertible debenture, or contingent agreement to acquire the shares of Boréal RD—or to cause Boréal RD to redeem voting shares held by others—may be granted to Boréal Parent or any non-resident, thereby neutralizing subparagraphs 251(5)(b)(i) and (ii) as well as the associated corporation rules in paragraph 256(1.2)(f) and subsection 256(1.4).

Simultaneously, the trustees of the trust and the directors of Boréal RD must be Canadian-resident individuals—such as the independent academic scientists who invented the LPHN chemistry alongside independent Canadian biotech executives—who are completely independent of, and deal at arm's length with, Boréal Parent. The trust deed must contain no "Protector" power in favour of Boréal Parent and no clause tying trustee eligibility to employment or directorship with Boréal Parent. Boréal RD must also appoint its own dedicated Chief Executive Officer, Director of Finance, and Corporate Secretary with zero personnel overlap with Boréal Parent's officers.
Step 2: Re-Engineering the Commercial & IP Licensing Agreement (Eliminating Economic Dependence and "Contract Payments")

To ensure Boréal RD is neither controlled in fact under subsections 256(5.1) and 256(5.11) nor stripped of its ITCs via the "contract payment" rules in subsection 127(9), Boréal RD must retain 100% legal and beneficial ownership of the core LPHN nanomedicine platform and patents. Rather than acting as a single-client contract research organization for Boréal Parent, Boréal RD must position its LPHN platform as a multi-indication delivery vehicle and enter into simultaneous research collaborations or material evaluation agreements with multiple Canadian universities and unrelated biotech firms across distinct therapeutic verticals, such as ocular delivery, oncology, and rare metabolic disorders.

Instead of receiving weekly R&D funding advances under a terminable research service contract, Boréal RD should raise seed or Series A equity from Canadian-resident angel networks and Canadian-controlled venture funds to self-fund its preclinical SR&ED. Boréal RD can then grant Boréal Parent a narrow, arm's-length commercial field-of-use option to negotiate a commercial license for a single specific neurological target after Boréal RD achieves preclinical proof-of-concept at its own risk and expense. Because Boréal Parent is not paying Boréal RD to perform SR&ED on its behalf, no "contract payment" arises under subsection 127(9), and because Boréal Parent cannot unilaterally terminate Boréal RD's multi-partner platform operations, economic dependence under Lyrtech RD Inc. is eliminated.
Step 3: Facility, Equipment, and Financial Accounting Segregation

To withstand CRA scrutiny of intercompany operations and section 37 expenditure claims, Boréal RD must lease dedicated wet-lab bench and vivarium space inside an independent Canadian biotechnology incubator (for example, in Laval or Toronto) under a direct commercial lease executed in its own name. Where Boréal RD utilizes specialized analytical instruments—such as cryo-transmission electron microscopy or LC-MS/MS mass spectrometers—owned by third parties or by Boréal Parent, usage must be governed by a formal written Core Facility Access Agreement billed strictly on an arm's-length hourly or per-sample market tariff supported by automated instrument usage logs, never via an employee headcount ratio. All reagents, ionizable lipids, microfluidic mixing cartridges, and animal models consumed or transformed in SR&ED under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and (II) must be ordered via Boréal RD's own purchase orders, delivered to Boréal RD's receiving dock, and tracked in a dedicated barcoded chemical inventory ledger.
Step 4: Structuring Experimentation Tracking to Distinguish Systematic SR&ED from Routine Screening

To prevent the CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) from disqualifying Project Neuro-Carrier as routine high-throughput formulation screening under subsection 248(1), Boréal RD must implement a structured Electronic Laboratory Notebook (ELN) protocol that tracks the scientific method contemporaneously. First, the ELN project charter must explicitly document the underlying scientific uncertainty by explaining why existing PEGylated lipid nanoparticles fail to cross the endothelial tight junctions of the blood-brain barrier without inducing complement-activation-related pseudoallergy (CARPA) or premature hepatic clearance, establishing that the relationship between biodegradable zwitterionic polymer chain length, surface zeta potential (−10 mV to +10 mV), and receptor-mediated transcytosis across human brain microvascular endothelial cells (hBMECs) cannot be predicted from published scientific literature or standard formulation practices.

Second, rather than testing random combinations of lipids through blind trial-and-error, every experimental batch in the ELN must state a mechanistic causal hypothesis before synthesis begins. For instance, Hypothesis B-12 should specify that incorporating a cleavable disulfide linker at the C-14 acyl tail position alongside a 3.5 mol% polysorbate-80 corona modification will maintain particle polydispersity index (PDI) below 0.2 under microfluidic shear stress while increasing trans-endothelial electrical resistance (TEER)-validated BBB permeability by 30% and reducing hepatic Kupffer cell uptake by 40% compared to baseline Formulation B-09. Third, for each batch synthesized, the ELN must automatically link raw dynamic light scattering (DLS) particle-size distributions, zeta-potential measurements, in vitro hBMEC transcytosis assay readouts, and endosomal escape fluorescence data, accompanied by a mandatory Causal Analysis & Scientific Advancement Note authored by the Principal Scientist analyzing the physicochemical mechanism of any formulation failure before authorizing the next synthesis cycle. Finally, every ELN experiment ID must be cross-referenced to the weekly timesheets of the specific biochemists performing the assays and to the exact lot numbers of custom lipids consumed, creating an unassailable contemporaneous audit trail linking technological uncertainty, systematic experimentation, independent corporate governance, and qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsections 37(1), 125(7), 127(9), 127(10.1), and 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (Canada).
Summary Matrix of Remedial Governance, Contractual, and Technical Controls

The table below synthesizes the remedial restructuring controls across both industry case studies in direct response to the statutory failures identified in Lyrtech RD Inc. v. The Queen (2013 TCC 12).

headers: Fatal Vulnerability in Lyrtech RD Inc. (2013 TCC 12)
Remedial Control in Case Study 1 (St-Laurent Photon-DSP)
Remedial Control in Case Study 2 (Boréal Nanomedicine)

cells: Shareholding & Trust Architecture (s. 125(7) & s. 251(5)(b))
Voting shares held by discretionary trust (FFL) settled by subsidiary of public parent; corporate beneficiaries were subsidiaries of Lyrtech Inc.
Trust eliminated; at least 75% of voting shares held directly by independent Canadian founders and private investors; SLT PubCo capped at 20% passive equity with no options.
Side-letter share option cancelled to defeat s. 251(5)(b)(i); corporate beneficiaries removed from trust; trust settled and controlled solely by arm's-length Canadian scientists.
Board & Officer Independence (s. 256(5.1) & CBCA s. 146(2))
FFL trust deed automatically removed any trustee who ceased to be a director of Lyrtech Inc.; s. 146(2) CBCA declaration stripped board powers; identical officers.
Independent Board of Directors; zero officer or director overlap with SLT PubCo; no s. 146(2) CBCA declaration vesting powers in parent fiduciaries.
Abolition of "Protector" and employment-linked trustee removal clauses in trust deed; separate CEO, Finance Director, and Secretary with zero overlap.
Debt Capitalization & Accounting (s. 256(5.1) & IT-64R4)
$1,016,437 demand promissory note issued on redemption of Class C shares and cycled to FFL; consolidated financial statements.
Equipment financed via commercial bank facilities or 5-year fixed-maturity subordinated debt with no demand feature; no IFRS consolidation.
Self-funded via Canadian seed/Series A private equity and venture capital rather than weekly parent cash advances; independent financial statements.
Commercial Autonomy & IP Ownership (s. 256(5.1) & s. 127(9))
Lyrtech Inc. retained all IP; single client; 60-day unilateral termination right; contingent 10%/25% royalty structure.
RD Lab owns 100% of core/foreground IP; multi-client licensing mandate; 60-day termination clause replaced with multi-year commercial supply agreement.
Boréal RD owns multi-indication LPHN platform and collaborates with multiple partners; Boréal Parent holds only a post-proof-of-concept field-limited commercial option.
Facilities & Expense Tracking (s. 37, s. 127(9) & s. 248(1))
Shared premises ($15,848/month) with no written lease and zero rent in 2005; 43/79 headcount allocation including parent's life insurance and audit fees.
Separate facility or formal written sublease at market rent; independent ledger and audit; PPA proxy overhead election (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)); weekly SR&ED timesheets.
Direct commercial wet-lab lease in biotech incubator; hourly/per-sample tariff for external core instruments; barcoded reagent tracking tied to hypothesis-driven ELN logs.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; court ruled the corporation was controlled by a public entity and ineligible for the enhanced CCPC rate.
